Fagan calls what his insurer, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois, is doing “malicious compliance.” He’s an associate professor of political science at the University of Illinois Chicago and uses his wife’s advocacy as an example to students.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Too good to be true</h3><p>Grano’s experience isn’t isolated. So many calls pour in to Chicago Family Doulas when the doula benefit starts this year that Rodney, its owner, hires an extra employee to answer them. But most of the time, families can’t get straight answers from their insurers and can’t afford a doula otherwise, she says.</p><p>“Every once in a while I see that somebody got coverage, and I’m like, “Oh my gosh, that’s insane,” Rodney says. “We’ll ask them, ‘What did you do?’ But I almost think it’s like a fluke or working really, really hard resubmitting, resubmitting.”</p><p>She mentions a rare success story of sorts: Katie Lombardi and her husband Louis Massard. Their daughter Clara was born in May, joining big sister Elia, who is 3.</p><p>Lombardi verifies with their insurer, Blue Cross, multiple times that they are eligible for a postpartum doula, she tells WBEZ. Customer service representatives never mention having to use a doula in-network, she says.</p><p>“The whole thing honestly seemed too good to be true,” says Lombardi, who lives in Andersonville on the North Side.</p><p>They hire a doula who tends to Clara overnight — feeding and swaddling her, washing bottles, folding laundry — as the family tries to get their older kiddo to sleep and to rest themselves. She comes twice, then Lombardi and Massard hit pause in a moment of panic after Blue Cross indicates they won’t cover it.</p><p>Then a check arrives in the mail reimbursing them. So they decide to try again and hire another overnight doula, who comes around twice a week for a few weeks. Their total cost out of pocket: about $4,500.</p><p>Again, Massard submits claims to Blue Cross. Some are fully paid. Others are not. It doesn’t make sense why, he says.</p><p>“This just reinforces why so many people don’t trust insurance companies,” Lombardi says. “You feel like insurance companies are almost never making decisions that are in the interest of their real customers, people like us on the other side of it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a5a54d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c385840/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec75c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Eleanor Grano stands on the back porch of her Riverside home on Sept. 15, 2026. Grano has spent nearly her entire pregnancy trying to access doula benefits. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec75c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f70c72a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec75c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F49%2F405affcc4ca681c95bb89d8521af%2Fdoulalaw-260927-004.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Throughout months of messages with her insurer, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois, Eleanor Grano’s frustration grew. A new state law requires private insurers cover the cost of doulas. But Grano learned she’d have to pay up front and then ask for reimbursement. The cost: around $10,000 for a month of overnight stays. Grano and her husband feared they would never get paid back.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Like Grano, Massard spends hours going back and forth with Blue Cross, navigating an alphabet soup of billing codes and receipts. He includes detailed cover sheets to help Blue Cross understand the claims he submits. Four claims have been reimbursed so far after a cycle of angry calls and messages, he explains.</p><p>Blue Cross still owes them about $1,800 and is trying to claw back around $1,800 it already reimbursed, Massard says.</p><p>He’s an attorney and writes an appeal to Blue Cross citing the Birth Equity Initiative and asking for an explanation of why the same claims for the same services are being treated differently.</p><p>“The best you can hope for after a contentious phone call with them is that the status online will change the following day, and then maybe maybe a week later they might issue a check — or they might issue a check and then a week later ask for their money back,” Massard says.</p><p>Ament declined to discuss Lombardi and Massard’s experience.</p><h3>‘There is no meaningful oversight’</h3><p>One of the reasons some families can’t get doulas paid for is because the majority of people in Illinois with private insurance have plans the state can't regulate, according to the Illinois Department of Insurance. For these families, their insurers aren’t required by the state to cover doulas, though they can, says Caron Brookens, a spokesperson for the state insurance department.</p><p>What’s more, for people whose insurers are required by the Birth Equity Initiative to cover doula services, legislators left a key part out of the law. They did not create a standard for how many doulas insurers must have in their networks or how far people have to travel to access one, Brookens confirms.</p><p>Insurers must meet what’s called a “network adequacy” standard for other types of providers in their networks, from pediatricians to orthopedic surgeons. Without one for doulas, insurers can decide how many they contract with as part of their networks.</p><p>If it’s a small pool, families might have to do what Grano and Lombardi did: find an out-of-network doula, pay them if they can, then try to get reimbursed by their insurer.</p><p>It’s confusing for families who see politicians tout the benefit of the Birth Equity Initiative: no cost-sharing.</p><p>Without a standard for doulas, insurers don’t have to tell state insurance regulators how many are in their networks. They also don’t have to say how much in claims they’ve paid for doula services, the department responded to a WBEZ public records request. That makes it hard to know if and where there are gaps in access.</p><p>“The implementation of the law on … private insurance has been lacking, and on private insurance I think there is no meaningful oversight,” says Kathy Waligora, deputy director of external affairs at EverThrive Illinois, a statewide advocacy group for maternal and child health. “It’s not clear that there are enough doulas to have an adequate network, but you could start trying. You could start trying to hold these companies to these standards.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-290000" name="image-290000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a2cdf46/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cc7eaa9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e28ff3c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois State. Rep. Robyn Gabel speaks about the importance of the bill during the signing of a birth equity legislation at Chicago Beyond in West Loop, Monday, July 29, 2024. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e28ff3c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d2936f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e28ff3c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5088x2856+0+268/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7b%2F3f%2F54a22278460986dab075e68cbccd%2Fpritzkersigning-073024-04.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Presented with WBEZ’s findings, Democrat state Rep. Robyn Gabel, a lead sponsor of the Birth Equity Initiative, says she plans to advance a bill in January that would fix a major shortcoming in the law.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gabel, a lead sponsor of the law, says the bill she plans to file in January would require network adequacy for doulas.</p><p>“There needs to be a little more pressure to make sure that the insurance companies recruit doulas and make sure that they have doulas in their networks,” Gabel says.</p><p>Ann Gillespie, director of the state insurance department, declined an on-the-record interview. The department is charged with implementing and enforcing the law.</p><p>Stratton, who spearheaded the law, also declined an interview request.</p><p>In response to questions, Brookens says the department can investigate complaints and encourages families and providers to file them. The state also audits insurers to see if they violate the law. But any violations for doula coverage likely won't be reported until 2027 or 2028 because the state typically reviews at least a full year of records, and the doula benefit for private insurance is new.</p><p>Grano’s complaint is one of a few related to doula services filed with the state. The department would not provide them, citing confidentiality.</p><p>Rodney says it’s a big ask for her more than 500 doulas to apply to join insurance networks. They’re independent contractors, not employees. It’s a cumbersome and time-consuming process.</p><p>And she wonders how much insurers would reimburse her doulas and how long it would take them to get paid. Some live paycheck to paycheck.</p><p>Insurers taking weeks, even months to pay providers is a <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/billions-in-profits-millions-in-unpaid-claims-medicaid-insurers-leave-illinois-providers-struggling-patients-losing-care/" target="_blank" ><u>common complaint</u></a>. Now Rodney pays her doulas weekly after they work with families.</p><h3>Blue Cross relents </h3><p>After WBEZ reached out to Blue Cross this fall about Grano’s experience, the insurer expedited her case and added her doula to its network. She and Fagan no longer have to pay $10,000 up front and risk not getting paid back.</p><p>Now they have 16 visits with a postpartum doula, half as many as Blue Cross originally said. This is a potential limit laid out in the law.</p><p>“Am I still worried that they’re not going to pay up? Yes,” Fagan says. “We’re going to fight it” if they don’t.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-240000" name="image-240000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e23f974/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/35a8f95/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/656b3eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Eleanor Grano sits in the kitchen of her Riverside home on Sept. 15, 2026. Grano has spent nearly her entire pregnancy trying to access doula benefits." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/656b3eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c399fcd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/656b3eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5542x3110+0+293/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fec%2F971c5198411a9357b2225469f760%2Fdoulalaw-260927-009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“If we want to show up for mothers … we can’t just pass these bills that say this colorful language and it’s so beautiful, but then not show up for the implementation,” says Eleanor Grano. She spent nearly her entire pregnancy trying to get her insurance company to cover a benefit Grano knew she was legally entitled to.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Grano worries other families can’t spend as much time as she has battling for a legal benefit.</p><p>“I definitely did not think it was going to take, what, nine months of contacting my health insurance to get it covered,” she says. “I can’t imagine what ordinary family has that type of time on their hands.”</p><p>She’s frustrated that Democrats tout the progressive values of living in a politically blue state, yet the finish line comes not when they pass laws, but when families can use them, she says.</p><p>“I’m excited,” Grano says,” to tell my daughter about what I got to do during her pregnancy — to fight for not just me.”</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/07/29/pritzker-signing-ceremony-legislation-expansion-abortion-coverage-black-maternal-deaths" >Pritzker signs measure to expand abortion coverage, combat Black maternal deaths</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Greg McCarty, beloved parking garage attendant at lakefront condo building, dies at 74
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Greg McCarty had a superpower.</p><p>Residents at 3900 N. Lake Shore Drive, the condo building where Mr. McCarty worked for 48 years as a parking attendant, knew it well.</p><p>He made people feel special.</p><p>A typical garage interaction unfolded one recent morning when Mr. McCarty saw resident Lauren Sauer and announced "Hey, just so you know." </p><p>He then broke into the Stevie Wonder song "I Just Called to Say I Love You."</p><p>Sauer, a real estate agent and former professional singer, took the cue.</p><p>"He loved to sing — could be Stevie or anything, really — and he and I would harmonize together in the garage," Sauer said.</p><p>He had this power to make people feel special," Sauer said."I've never met anyone like him before."</p><p>Broad, over six feet tall, and possessing an easy smile, Mr. McCarty performed duties far beyond parking and retrieving cars.</p><p>He helped with groceries, held doors, washed cars, filled tires that needed air, fixed home appliances and identified any car issues and suggested reputable cars mechanics.</p><p>"He never was looking for a tip," said Doug Silverstein, a resident and former hospital administrator. "He’d be embarrassed if you ever tried to give him money."</p><p>During quiet times in the garage, he sometimes drew flowers with colored pencils and gifted his creations to building residents.</p><p>"I have one on my fridge," Sauer said. "It's funny you don't think of a garage valet as someone who's going to become a key person in your daily life, but he truly was a wonderful guy." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div> </div><p>Mr. McCarty died Aug. 18 after suffering a heart attack. He was 74.</p><p>"Everybody in the building seemed to have a relationship with Greg," said Bill Wheelhouse, former state capitol bureau chief for Illinois Public Radio in Springfield. "Mine just started talking sports and basketball, and I wasn't even that big of a basketball fan."</p><p>Wheelhouse got skybox tickets to a Chicago Bulls game and invited Mr. McCarty.</p><p>"He was really kind of one of my first acquaintances and friends when we moved to Chicago a few years ago," said Wheelhouse, whose wife, in tribute, put flowers on the ledge of a flowerbed outside the building where Mr. McCarty sat during the quiet moments of his shift.</p><p>Soon more flowers and balloons were left there, too.</p><p>"We're going to have a memorial plaque put at that spot to honor him, with a little ceremony to unveil it in January," said Luther Goins, a theater producer and director who lives in the building.</p><p>"He made all of us feel that life was a little better for meeting a guy like this," said Goins. "And he was a stunning example of someone who was committed to his job."</p><p>Mr. McCarty, who grew up in a small town in Mississippi and in Chicago, lived in South Shore with his wife, Evadney McCarty.</p><p>"They met when they lived in the same building and she asked him to fix a light bulb because he was tall," said Mr. McCarty's nephew, Fabian Higgins.</p><p>"He was very old school, didn't have a credit card or any debt, took great care of the things in his life, like his Eddie Bauer-edition Ford Explorer, which had more than 300,000 miles on it when it finally died out this summer," Higgins said.</p><p>"And he was very loyal and committed, especially to his wife, he loved her and did a lot for her," Higgins said.</p><p>As a kid, he was in a singing group that loved to perform songs by The Temptations, his family said.</p><p>More than a dozen building residents attended Mr. McCarty's funeral, and more than 100 wrote cards to his family.</p><p>"Greg was a gentle giant," said his sister, Sherrie Gamblin. </p><p>"What you see is what you get with Greg, and I love him like a brother," said Henry L. James, a colleague who has worked as a parking attendant at the building for nearly as long as Mr. McCarty.</p><p>Mr. McCarty is survived by his wife, Evadney McCarty, and his sisters, Betty Forbes and Sherrie Gamblin.</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: Giant puppets and dozens of dancers will fuel Chicago’s Arts in the Dark Parade
entries.summary: <p>As the sun sets on Saturday night, Chicago's Columbus Drive will come alive with a fire-breathing dragon, giant animal puppets, and scores of drumlines and dance troupes.  </p><p>The annual Arts in the Dark parade, now in its 12th year, is not your typical parade. No politicians, no beauty queens, no groups in matching T-shirts tossing candy in the hot, noon sun. Instead, this night of spooky festivity is all about putting on a performance and celebrating parading as an art form, said Mark Kelly, the event’s co-founder and artistic director.</p><p>“It's about as close as you're going to come to Mardi Gras in Chicago,” said Kelly, the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/7/13/22576284/department-of-cultural-affairs-and-special-events-commissioner-mark-kelly-retire-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>former cultural commissioner</u></a>. “It's not Mardi Gras, but it sort of captures that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-credit"><p>Contributed</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Last year, both rainy weather and Operation Midway Blitz dampened the parade’s festive flare. But one year later, there’s an enthusiastic spirit among the roughly 100 groups set to participate. In total, they’ll bring nearly 5,000 performers, ranging from high school marching bands to an all-women lowrider car club. Plus, there will be giant alebrijes, a 60-foot glow worm, circus acts and ballet folklórico dancers.</p><p>It’s meant to celebrate the city’s vibrant diversity. Plus, for Kelly, it’s a chance to embrace Halloween as an artist’s holiday.</p><p>“It's the purest of all of the holidays in this country, and we're declaring it as ours,” Kelly said. “Think of it as, entries.title: Griffin MSI defends its criticized Welcome Hall design
entries.summary: <p>The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry contemplated seven glassy and visually transparent Welcome Hall designs before selecting the one now criticized as too big and obstructive for the landmark site.</p><p>"I think there was a little bit of tension — a healthy tension — between it being just sort of the Apple Store glass monument and this beautiful Charles Atwood historic neoclassical building, or something that had some commonality [with the museum]," RAMSA Associate Partner Caitlin Getman, the project's lead designer, said.</p><p>Getman said the chosen design achieves "compatibility that ... clearly distinguishes itself as different" from the museum building.</p><p>The schemes were shown to me during an exclusive 90-minute interview Monday with Griffin MSI CEO Chevy Humphrey, Getman and the project's preservation consultant Emily Ramsey.</p><p>The museum wouldn't make the seven renderings available for publication, though. A spokesperson said the renderings were "early drafts" that showed "all the evolution that’s happened."</p><p>But during our talk, Humphrey, Getman and Ramsey shared new images and diagrams of the Welcome Hall planned for the front lawn of the museum's 57th Street main entrance.</p><p>They said the hall, which would link to the museum by way of a glass connection through the middle of the building’s exterior front stairs, would architecturally enhance the 133-year-old Greek Revival beauty.</p><p>They also said the 28-foot tall, 458-foot wide hall would provide admission-free public spaces, with galleries and restrooms, and make it easier for the museum's 1.5 million yearly visitors to enter the building.</p><p>"There needs to be free spaces and places where people feel that they are welcome [and that] this is their museum," Humphrey said. "That's been the whole ultimate goal of this whole process."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Hall in front of the Hyde Park museum.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The project has caught flack since renderings were released last month. I called the proposed building "<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" target="_blank" >a big old wide-brimmed hat blocking the screen at the movie theater</a>."</p><p>Others have criticized the building too, including noted Chicago author and historian Tim Samuelson. </p><p>In a Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/09/23/griffin-museum-of-science-and-industry-cta-artificial-intelligence-ai" target="_blank" >letter to the editor</a>, Samuelson said the hall and the museum's new South Portico renovation "display gross disrespect for a masterpiece ... nearly perfect in composition, proportions and detail."</p><p>I've got no beef with the South Portico project. Sure, it's a secondary entrance, but it shows restraint and a sense of proportion that the Welcome Hall lacks.</p><p>Ramsey said the hall "creates this sense of welcome for people who are not necessarily architecture buffs, who don't necessarily have the same appreciation for very strict, and some would say, forbidding, classical architecture."</p><p>The seven previously considered Welcome Hall images I saw were not as elaborately rendered as the approved design, so its hard to say which of them might have been a better alternative.</p><p>But the renderings do show the Griffin MSI and RAMSA at least considered more purely glass designs. Some that — to my eye at least — resembled the transparency of the <a class="Link" href="https://inhabitat.com/glassy-renovation-brings-natural-light-into-canadian-museum-of-nature/" target="_blank" >2010 addition</a> atop Ottawa's century-old Canadian Museum of Nature, or the Portland Art Museum's 22,000-square-foot Mark Rothko <a class="Link" href="https://portlandartmuseum.org/campus-transformation/" target="_blank" >entrance pavilion.</a></p><p>"There was no stone unturned, in terms of different architectural ideas," Getman said.</p><p>The new images provided for publication show a grass-topped 152-foot wide central entryway flanked by landscaped berms — they will contain service rooms — that stretch out like arms toward the museum's existing east and west pavilions.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fa0000" entries.title: Woman has baby. Baby sprouts black feathers. Horror ensues.
entries.summary: <p>Your baby is cooing, babbling, taking her first tottery steps — all of it making you deliriously happy.</p><p>She is absolutely perfect.</p><p>But wait, what is that splinter-like black thing sticking out of her plump, soft skin? You frantically thumb through the Bible for new parents: the American Academy of Pediatrics “Caring for Your Baby and Young Child.”</p><p>Or, if you are Nora Pacetti, you ask your mother because, being an Italian mamma, her knowledge of raising children eclipses that of a hospital full of pediatricians. But even Nonna Pacetti can’t figure this one out. And now, to Nora’s horror, another black needle has pierced her baby’s skin. And another.</p><p>“Pinfeathers” ($30, Berkley; out Nov. 17) is a delightfully unsettling read — a witch’s brew, blending a generous helping of David Cronenberg’s 1986 horror classic, “The Fly,” with a dash of “Rosemary’s Baby,” as well as a pinch of “X-Men.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>North Side author Christina Henry’s latest horror novel probably isn’t for an expectant mother because no infant Tylenol, extra fluids or a warm bath is going to stop baby Olivia’s prickly nubs from sprouting into feathers or the hard, sharp thing inside her throat lunging out to grab a sandwich, a finger or anything else juicy within reach.</p><p>“Despite the fact that there is this very unusual thing happening to [Nora’s] daughter, the book actually is really just an expression of the parental anxiety around illness, difficulty, things that you don’t expect when you become a parent,” said Henry, looking suitably witchy, her ebony-dark hair streaked silver, black nail polish and a black cardigan decorated with toadstools and dragonflies.</p><p>We’re chatting at a favorite hangout, Hexe Coffee, located in the old Lathrop public housing project at 2000 W. Diversey Parkway. She’s wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “I like books more than people.” But if she is a witch, she’s a friendly, engaging one.</p><p>“Pinfeathers” is Henry’s 20th novel. Many, but not all, are set in Chicago.</p><p>“I’ve had a very strange career, in that I’m not a household name, but my books sell consistently and they keep selling,” Henry said.</p><p>Her latest begins within the claustrophobic confines of a North Side condominium. But a baby morphing into — spoilers here and below — a huge condor-eagle hybrid doesn’t belong in a condo. Olivia belongs in a secret lab, or so the ruthless Dr. Noel Cassidy believes, to be poked, prodded and possibly plucked. Maddeningly for Dr. Cassidy, clinical efficiency is no match for a mother’s love or a grandmother’s paranoia.</p><p>Henry, the mother of a 20-year-old engineering student, said the idea of a baby sprouting feathers came to her, like the central theme of all of her books, from the “primordial ooze” in her brain.</p><p>“Like a perfectly normal person, I have to write a book to find out what I’m seeing in my head,” she said.</p><p>Henry grew up in New York’s Hudson Valley, an “unmonitored” Gen-Xer.</p><p>“Horror was part of my childhood in a really visceral way,” she said. “Nobody really paid attention to what we were watching and what we were reading.”</p><p>Henry and her teenage friends clung to each other during sleepovers and screamed through the likes of “A Nightmare on Elm Street,” “Dead Ringers” and “Halloween.”</p><p>Master horror storyteller Shirley Jackson and English gothic horror writer Angela Carter are among her influences.</p><p>“Stephen King is sort of an overarching influence on probably every horror author who came out of the ’80s because he was so ubiquitous,” Henry said.</p><p>Henry crafts her own stories at home in her Wrigleyville graystone, so close to the home of the Cubs that, “when the wind blows in from the east, I can hear the seventh-inning stretch,” she said.</p><p>She writes by hand — at least to begin with.</p><p>“It helps me access a deeper part of my brain,” she said. “I don’t plan out my books. I just start writing them.”</p><p>But Wrigleyville feels like an odd place for a horror writer to settle and find inspiration, too much noise and bustle at all hours for ghosts or axe murderers to feel at home.</p><p>Not so, said Henry. In fact, her last novel, “The Place Where They Buried Your Heart,” is set in an abandoned house in Wrigleyville, a home drenched in generations of human blood.</p><p>“It is really a love letter to the neighborhood in a strange sort of way,” Henry said.</p>

entries.title: Months after storm, Gary residents are plagued with blackouts
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was originally published in </i><a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/gary-intermittent-power-outages-nipsco/" target="_blank" ><i>Capital B Gary</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>After some Gary residents endured two to three weeks without electricity in August, many are still living with uncertainty.</p><p>Residents contacted by Capital B report experiencing intermittent power disruptions even after power was restored to the city following the storm. They said they fear their lights will flicker and go dark during rains or high winds. They worry their refrigerators will go silent for several hours, sometimes even days, and food will spoil.</p><p>Residents say there were occasional power outages before the Aug. 11 storm. But the hardship of enduring a weekslong blackout has made recent interruptions even more unbearable.</p><p>“The August 11 derecho was an unprecedented storm that caused extraordinary damage across northern Indiana, and we understand many customers and communities continue to recover from its effects,” NIPSCO said in a statement to Capital B Gary. “We understand that reliable electric service is important to our customers and the communities we serve.”</p><p>Resident Sherry Smith remembers the August storm as if it were yesterday. The former Gary Common Council employee was without power for two weeks after the storm, and she said the recurring blackouts constantly keep her on edge that she’ll be plunged into darkness again.</p><p>“We need to take this seriously because we’re still having power out,” she said.</p><p>“Every time it rains, I’m thinking that my power may go out,” Smith said. “Those trees may fall on the wires, and my neighbors’ electricity will go out again.”</p><p>She’s not alone.</p><p>Westside resident and business owner Marsha Jones says her power goes out whenever it rains. After the storm struck, her lights remained dark for 19 days, water damaged her basement, and her roof leaks from two holes.</p><p>“It’s something that I never had to deal with before,” she said.</p><p>Jones hasn’t slept in her house in more than two months. Instead, she has been staying with her mother, who hasn’t experienced any other blackouts. Luckily, her business, MJ’s Boutique, avoided damage from the Aug. 11 storm and hasn’t experienced disruptions since power was restored. But she misses sleeping in her own bed.</p><p>“I want to go home,” she said. “I just want to go back to how life was before the storm.”</p><p>Jones’ frustrations are compounded by the impact on her checkbook. Her utility bill is twice what she expected to pay after almost three weeks without power. She said she spoke with NIPSCO and was told someone would come out to check her meter to see why the bill was so high.</p><p>She said she’s still waiting.</p><p>“They need to be held accountable,” Jones said. “I’m just praying for us to get back to normal.”</p><h3>Persistent power outages</h3><p>Gary Councilman Myles Tolliver Sr., who lives in Miller, said the problem predates the storm: Power interruptions have become the norm.</p><p>“The wind blows the wrong way, we lose power,” said Tolliver, whose electricity has been interrupted four times since the storm. “We might lose power for six to seven hours if the wind blows, and if it rains, we might lose power for a day or so.”</p><p>Tolliver has lost power while preparing for council meetings or while his kids do their homework. Sometimes the lights are not restored until later in the evening. Like the others, he called NIPSCO to inquire about the situation but got no explanation, only an estimated restoration time.</p><p>The utility’s failure to properly maintain power lines may be causing the problem, Tolliver said.</p><p>“If you go and just ride around the Miller area, or really Gary as a whole … you can see that the lines are embedded in tree limbs and leaves,” Tolliver said. “There are trees that were marked to be cut years ago that haven’t been cut. No maintenance has been happening.”</p><p>While he’s seen some work done, he said more is needed so Gary residents don’t have to deal with these problems, especially after storms.</p><p>After the storm, Tolliver’s house was without electricity for two and a half weeks. Without a working refrigerator, his family lost all their food.</p><p>Tolliver sent his family to a hotel outside Chicago. While they were away, he spent much of his time assisting residents in the community.</p><p>“It was some things that I don’t know if I’ll ever see again, but it was definitely life-changing,” he said. “I had to be there because they’re depending on me. It’s the reason why I’m in office to serve and make sure they get what they need.”</p><h3>Shopping differently for food</h3><p>As Gary residents struggle to recover, the memory of the lengthy power outage, combined with untimely interruptions in electric service since then, has changed how they live.</p><p>“I think everybody’s feeling that way, and I think it’s changed the trajectory of how we save food,” Tolliver said.</p><p>With nearly 40% of Gary residents receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, the community faces another layer of uncertainty.</p><p>“When I look at things differently now, I never save food as I used to,” Tolliver added. “Now it’s only buying enough to last a certain amount of time. But with food costs rising constantly and the approaching holiday/winter season, it’s hard to find a middle ground as circumstances change.”</p><p>The persistent outages led him, and many others in the Gary community, to push state officials for answers. In September, a <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/nipsco-statehouse-committee-hearing/" target="_blank" >joint committee</a> hearing at the Indiana Statehouse examined NIPSCO’s storm preparedness and response. There, Tolliver joined fellow leaders and residents in expressing frustration with the utility’s handling of the disaster.</p><p>“I think for a lot of time, elected officials tiptoe around things, and that’s one thing that I’m not going to do: I’m going to speak my truth,” Tolliver said.</p><p>Smith woke up around 4 a.m. to drive almost three hours from Gary to the Statehouse in Indianapolis to tell lawmakers about the frequent power outages.</p><p>“This happened before the derecho. It happened during the derecho, and it’s still happening as we get ready to come into the winter months,” she said while speaking on the House floor.</p><p>The weekend before her testimony, Smith said, her power went out around 11:30 a.m. Saturday and returned around 4 p.m. The following day, it went out again between 1:30 a.m. and 4 a.m.</p><p>“It wasn’t any type of storm or anything,” she recalled. “It was a nice day, and the power just went out.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago passengers could see fuel surcharge on taxi fares
entries.summary: <p>Chicago taxi drivers can now charge riders a fuel surcharge, as gas prices remain high in the city.</p><p>The fuel surcharge went into effect Wednesday and was authorized by the Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection.</p><p>The surcharge is implemented when both the AAA’s current average and month ago average price for regular gasoline in the Chicago area reaches $5 per gallon or more.</p><p>Taxi drivers can charge $1 if the fare is $20 or less; $2 for fares between $20.01 and $40; and $3 for fares $40.01 or more. The surcharge applies to the fare before taxes, tolls and additional fees are added.</p><p>City officials said a notice must be posted inside the cab.</p><p>The surcharge will remain in effect until gas prices drop below the required threshold. A previous <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/20/amid-changing-industry-chicago-cabbies-and-ride-hailing-drivers-are-both-struggling-im-stuck-in-this" >taxi</a> fuel surcharge was in place June 1-23.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/20/amid-changing-industry-chicago-cabbies-and-ride-hailing-drivers-are-both-struggling-im-stuck-in-this" >Amid changing industry, Chicago cabbies and rideshare drivers are both struggling</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Huntley man charged with possession of child sexual abuse materials
entries.summary: <p>A Huntley man was arrested earlier this week, accused of possession of child sexual abuse materials, authorities announced.</p><p>Jon M. Roth, 43, was arrested Tuesday and charged with 10 counts of possession of child sexual abuse materials for victims under 13 years old, according to the Huntley police department. </p><p>Roth, who was being held at the McHenry County Jail, is due back for a hearing at the McHenry County Courthouse on Oct. 27, court records show. </p><p>The Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force provided obtained information to the police department regarding a phone number registered to a person in Huntley who was attempting to upload potential child sexual abuse materials for download via a cloud-based online storage service, authorities said, adding that the investigation led to officials identifying Roth. </p><p>Authorities served a search warrant at Roth's home and was taken into custody based on evidence gained during the search, police said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/jon-roth-huntley-idd-man-charged-having-child-sex-abuse-materials-9800-block-williams-drive-police-say/19965826/" target="_blank" >ABC7Chicago</a> reported that Roth is a bus driver with Huntley School District 158. The district hasn’t yet responded to requests for comment. </p>

entries.title: Data centers will cost ComEd $3 billion but consumer groups worry Illinois households will be on the hook
entries.summary: <p>ComEd expects to spend more than $3 billion to connect data centers to its electric grid in the coming years, but it has only collected about one-fourth of the costs from data center developers — a troubling gap that could leave Illinois consumers on the hook, according to consumer groups.</p><p>The figures are from ComEd’s cost projections that were included with expert testimony this summer in a regulatory matter before the Illinois Commerce Commission. The expert testifying on behalf of the Citizens Utility Board, Environmental Law & Policy Center, National Resources Defense Counsel, Vote Solar and the Union of Concerned Scientists analyzed the utility’s cost projections, which are based on 30 large-load users.</p><p>The consumer advocates say that if the large-load data center projects don’t come to fruition after the utility has spent billions to connect them, Illinois households and small businesses could be left holding the bag — an assertion ComEd denies.</p><p>While companies associated with the 30 projects were redacted, the figures include more than $1.4 billion in new transmission work, $189 million in upgrades to existing transmission infrastructure and more than $1.5 billion to improve the distribution system, for a total of $3.1 billion in anticipated costs.</p><p>Deposits and advance payment commitments for these projects total $720.9 million.</p><p>The large-load users have been built in Illinois since 2021 or are expected to come online through 2031 and will need access to 50 megawatts or more of power — enough electricity for a small city.</p><p>That level of usage could describe a major industrial plant, but CUB believes the projects are data centers, which are being proposed around the country as part of the artificial intelligence boom.</p><p>CUB Executive Director Sarah Moskowitz says it’s unfair for tech corporations to not pay upfront and that “everyday electric customers are potentially on the hook for billions in higher bills” for system improvements.</p><p>CUB was created by the state legislature in 1983 as an independent, nonpartisan advocate for residential and small business utility customers.</p><p>A ComEd spokesman said the consumer groups’ analysis “is not complete and paints an inaccurate picture.”</p><p>The utility points to its new “Transmission Security Agreements” with large-load users that protect its spending on transmission work. Those agreements, approved by state and federal regulators, will “ensure that large-load customers cover the costs of serving them for the duration of the TSA, even if they go out of business or use substantially less energy than expected,” the spokesman said.</p><p>As for the $1.5 billion in distribution improvements, ComEd says it’s still working out what that infrastructure will cost and how much the large users will need to deposit.</p><p>“Some of these projects will not come online for five years, and ComEd’s engineering work needed to estimate the deposits is not yet complete. This means that the $721 million deposit amount may increase,” the utility’s spokesman says. He added that ComEd “supports the principle of cost allocation to large-load customers.”</p><p>ComEd also has asked the ICC for permission to throttle data centers’ service if the grid becomes too stressed, such as on very hot days.</p><p>But CUB and other consumer advocates say that’s not enough and Illinois leaders need to plan for a worst-case scenario, in which some of the projects don’t proceed and ComEd is left with stranded assets that still need to be paid off.</p><p>Nick Wallace, senior associate attorney at the Environmental Law & Policy Center, says the financial exposure for consumers could be even higher because there will likely be more data centers following the 30 in ComEd’s queue.</p><p>The groups are pushing Illinois lawmakers to pass the Protecting Our Water, Energy and Ratepayers Act, or POWER Act, which would require data centers to pay 100% of their costs before connecting to the grid.</p><p>The proposed legislation also includes protections against pollution and overuse of water.</p><p>Data centers’ outsized needs for energy and water — and the noise they produce — have upset people from across the political spectrum who say they don’t want them in their communities.</p><p>The pressure comes amid rising electric bills and consumer frustration over high prices for food, housing, healthcare and other essentials. ComEd’s electricity supply price is up about 50% compared to two years ago, according to CUB.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has voiced support for data center regulations, which could come up during the veto session in Springfield in mid-November and early December.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/09/18/metropolitan-water-reclamation-district-artificial-intelligence-hawthorne-race-course-stickney-cicero" >Hatred for data centers is sky high, but this local government agency sees dollar signs</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Derrick Rose embraces filmmaking in his post-hoops second act
entries.summary: <p>First it was flowers, now it’s film.</p><p>Less than two years after launching his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2025/01/02/chicago-bulls-derrick-rose-becomes-florist-for-a-day-handing-out-thousands-of-free-flowers-to-fans" target="_blank" ><u>pop-up floral business</u></a>, former Chicago Bulls player <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/making/2023/12/14/making-derrick-rose" target="_blank" >Derrick Rose </a>is building a career in the movie industry.</p><p>He is an executive producer of “<a class="Link" href="https://linktr.ee/3colorsfilm?utm_source=ig&utm_medium=social&utm_content=link_in_bio&fbclid=PAZXh0bgNhZW0CMTEAcGRvZgJzcnRjBmFwcF9pZA85MzY2MTk3NDMzOTI0NTkAAafi4jOXdFvjMeNUjUDfSvZG1mRgR9B0zEnv2-sVbflvTCimAt5V07o81dcC7w_aem_2MO_1YOvAPfxz-gJk0RsRg" target="_blank" >Three Colors: Pan-African</a>,” a narrative feature that just screened at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" >Chicago International Film Festival</a>. Directed by Elijah Davis, Tyler Ocasio Holmes and Allison A. Waite, the three-part anthology demonstrates the breadth of the Black experience.<b> </b></p><p>The film is a pivotal career marker for Rose, who previously produced the documentary <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/4/23383334/punch-9-for-harold-washington-review-documentary-chicago-mayor-movie-1983-election" >“Punch 9 for Harold Washington</a>,” in 2021. He also spearheaded projects about his own life, producing the documentary "Pooh: The Derrick Rose Story" in 2019 and directing the "Becoming a Rose" short film last year. He said he plans to tell more stories onscreen about Black history and culture, while expanding Rose’s Flower Shop and launching other ventures.</p><p>“Basketball never defined me, even though people thought it did,” said Rose, 38, who retired from the NBA in 2024.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4a0000" name="image-4a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bd5cacf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/873d7d8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd59a93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A young girl sits at the dining room table in a still from the "Three Colors: Pan-African" film. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd59a93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e444e22/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd59a93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3849x2160+74+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2Fa8%2F05615f244e8d80e8b2c2fcca74ab%2Fblack-approved-still-1.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A still from “Black: Breadman,” directed by Allison A. Waite. The segment is part of the anthology, “Three Colors: Pan-African,” which screened at the Chicago International Film Festival. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of the Chicago International Film Festival</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Named for each color of the Pan-African flag, the fictional stories in "Three Colors" cover a college football star reeling from an injury, an immigrant at risk of deportation and a TV actor trying not to compromise his morals.</p><p>The film was conceived by Davis, a Chicago native and son of longtime NBA ref Marc Davis, and it co-stars veteran actress Loretta Devine and local actor Bashir Salahuddin. Steppenwolf Theatre Artistic Director Glenn Davis and “Windfall” playwright <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/04/10/windfall-steppenwolf-play-tarell-alvin-mccraney-moonlight-writer" >Tarell Alvin McCraney</a> are also executive producers. </p><p>The movie has won awards at the Slamdance Film Festival and the American Black Film Festival.<br>The team is in talks with distributors to bring the film to theaters nationwide next year.</p><p>“Everything that I'm involving myself in right now are things that I thought about [over] 10 years ago," Rose said. "It’s just that, now, I have the time to be able to dive into these things and bring along my family to create these businesses.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c90000" name="image-c90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5fda4fb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+248/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F58%2Fb350fc7b4fe4a32800c39f84ba10%2Fbull-cst-041813-1.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bcf7026/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+248/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F58%2Fb350fc7b4fe4a32800c39f84ba10%2Fbull-cst-041813-1.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f8e7539/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+248/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F58%2Fb350fc7b4fe4a32800c39f84ba10%2Fbull-cst-041813-1.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Bulls Vs Washington Wizards. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Derrick Rose poses on the red carpet at the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts during the Chicago International Film Festival. The former basketball star said he is interested in documenting the lives of everyone from African emperors to other NBA players to unsung Black visual artists. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Rose was also impressed by the script, especially the story about the athlete, who faces an identity crisis, economic uncertainty and tension at home after getting hurt.</p><p>Directed by Davis, the segment — “Red: Black Men Don’t Cry” — resonates with Rose, who also dealt with injuries while playing basketball.</p><p>“When you are the breadwinner in the family, and you have turmoil, it can be pretty hard when those expectations turn into burdens,” Rose said. “For me, I had those expectations since I was in the sixth grade.”</p><p>Rose also said he could relate to “Green: Meet the Greens,” the segment about a TV actor, Jontavious (portrayed by Bashir Salahuddin), who is offered a lot of money to play a harmful Black stereotype. Like Jontavious, Rose also grappled with career decisions, such as rejecting certain endorsements, amid pressures to fit into a certain mold.</p><p>“The money coerces you,” he said. “It makes you go against your morals and your integrity. Waite, actor Bashir Salahuddin and director Elijah Davis pose on the red carpet ahead of the screening of "Three Colors: Pan-African" during the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eed13f4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fd9%2Fe3f74bad45e2abf732bd46c5cc46%2Frosefilm-261028-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ec4a63/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fd9%2Fe3f74bad45e2abf732bd46c5cc46%2Frosefilm-261028-10.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eed13f4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fd9%2Fe3f74bad45e2abf732bd46c5cc46%2Frosefilm-261028-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>From left, director Allison A. Waite, actor Bashir Salahuddin and director Elijah Davis pose on the red carpet ahead of the screening of “Three Colors: Pan-African” during the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival at AMC NEWCITY 14 on Oct. 15, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p> Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><p>As a Black actor in real life, Salahuddin said he is also careful about the types of roles he accepts.</p><p>“Now more than ever, as an actor, you have to be responsible for the work that you do,” said Salahuddin, who also starred in the beloved Chicago comedy series “South Side.”</p><p>“There certainly was a time when it was just work, but I think folks expect it to be a little more thoughtful now,” he said. “Luckily, especially when it comes to young filmmakers, they aren't even thinking about some of those old stereotypes and those old motives.”</p><p>Another young director out of USC, Allison A. Waite said she was thinking about nuances within the Black community for her segment, “Black: Breadman.” The protagonist, a Black immigrant, initially shuns the African American residents of her community.</p><p>“My film is about unity and what can happen when we put those prejudices aside and come together,” Waite said. “It's something that we don't really see that often, and I think it's an important part of understanding how we show up as Black people in the world.”</p><p>Also passionate about telling Black stories, Rose said he hopes to continue working with Davis to bring some of his ideas to the screen. He is interested in documenting the lives of everyone from African emperors to other NBA players. </p><p>And as a collector of Black art, he also wants to inform others about the unsung artists he has discovered.</p><p>“Those are stories that I love to figure out,” he said. “I love the untold stories.”</p>

JB Pritzker signed the Birth Equity Initiative in an attempt to prevent the deaths of new mothers. One key part was broadening access to doulas — trained professionals who support families, advocate on behalf of those giving birth in the delivery room, help with pain management, or take care of newborns. People with private insurance could have a doula with no cost-sharing. The message to families: You won’t have to pay.</p><p><b>The reality</b>: Private insurers were supposed to be ready to cover doulas on Jan. 1, but the law is still missing key pieces. Families are paying the price, according to a WBEZ investigation. And only an estimated 30% of people with private insurance in Illinois have plans the state can regulate. For everyone else, it could be much more difficult to access this benefit. In many cases, doula agencies say women stop trying to use insurance to pay for support because it's so much work.</p><p><b>For example</b>: A Chicago couple who had their baby girl about five months ago is still trying to get Blue Cross to fully reimburse them for their overnight doula. And the insurer is trying to claw back nearly $2,000 it already paid.</p><p><b>Vows to act</b>: Presented with WBEZ's findings, State Rep. Robyn Gabel, a lead sponsor of the initial legislation, said she plans to advance a bill that would fix a major shortcoming with the law.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yditudjd-l-h/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>PUBLIC SAFETY 🚨</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yditudjd-l-iy/" target="_blank" >Neil Steinberg</a></h5><p>A pumpkin seed weighs about 1/100th of an ounce, when planted in April. By late September that little oval the size of a fingernail can increase in size 18,000 times, into a 12-pound pumpkin, ready for picking.</p><p>"There are days, when the conditions are right, I’m pretty sure I can hear them grow," says John H. Ackerman, a fourth-generation farmer in downstate Morton, the self-proclaimed pumpkin capital of the world.</p><p>Morton seized the title, though Illinois could easily dub itself "Pumpkin Heaven" because the state grows so many of the fall icons.</p><p>In 2025, our state grew 535 million pounds of pumpkin, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. More than the next four top pumpkin-growing states — California, Indiana, Michigan and Pennsylvania — combined.</p><p>What makes Illinois so pumpkin-friendly?</p><p>One expert said it's a combination of Illinois' soil composition, climate and geography, plus the many multi-generational family farmers statewide.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yditudjd-l-ij/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition! entries.title: It's not too late to register to vote. Here's what you need to know to cast your ballot by Nov. 3.
entries.summary: <p>Election Day is less than two weeks away. But it's not too late to register to vote. </p><p>Here's everything you need to know about registering to vote in Illinois for the upcoming midterm elections. </p><h3>Who can register to vote? </h3><p>To vote in the Illinois, you must be: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0fb13a40-ce4e-11f1-95b2-ff2c48fd3bf0"><li>A U.S. citizen</li><li>18 years or older by the date of the general election</li><li>An Illinois resident for at least 30 days</li></ul><h3>Are you already registered to vote?</h3><p>You can check your voter registration status online on <a class="Link" href="https://ova.elections.il.gov/RegistrationLookup.aspx" target="_blank" >Illinois State Board of Elections website</a> or on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/" target="_blank" >Chicago Board of Elections’ website</a>.</p><h3>Need to register? It’s not too late! </h3><p>You can no longer register to vote online through the state's board of election website — Registration closes 16 days before Election Day.</p><p>But if you still need to register, you have several options to do so in person:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0fb13a41-ce4e-11f1-95b2-ff2c48fd3bf0"><li><b>Driver’s license renewal:</b> When applying for or renewing your driver’s license or state ID card at a DMV, you will be asked if you want to register to vote. If you answer yes, you will be required to attest, under penalty of perjury, that you meet the qualifications to register to vote and provide your electronic signature.<br></li><li><b>Municipal offices:</b> Multiple local government offices register voters in-person including the county clerk’s office, board of election commissioners office, city and village offices, township offices, and military recruitment offices.<br></li><li><b>Same day:</b> Illinois allows same day registration at early voting sites and on Election Day. You must bring <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/when-you-need-id-vote" target="_blank" >two forms of ID</a> or proof of residency. The state allows for several types of ID and proofs of residency: a passport, driver’s license, student ID, pay stub, lease, medical bill or mortgage. Here is <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/when-you-need-id-vote" target="_blank" >the full list of acceptable IDs</a>. At least one of them must list your current address. For example, your state driver's license with an old address plus a copy of a ComEd bill with your current address will work. </li></ul><h3>Have you moved since the last Election Day and need to change your registration? </h3><p>You can also change your registration the same day you vote. Follow the same instructions above for registering to vote. </p><h3>What to remember while voting</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0fb13a42-ce4e-11f1-95b2-ff2c48fd3bf0"><li>Ballots in other languages are available. Chicago and Cook County polling locations have voting machines that offer audio ballots in Arabic, Chinese (audio in Mandarin dialect), Gujarati, Hindi, Korean, Polish, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog, Ukrainian and Urdu.<br></li><li>You can bring notes, sample ballots and endorsements with you into a polling booth.<br></li><li>You can bring children with you to vote.<br></li><li>If you’re blind, physically disabled or unable to read or write, you can ask an election judge, friend, family member or another voter to help you complete your ballot. But that helper can’t be from your employer or union. The person also cannot influence your vote and cannot fill out your ballot without your expressed intent.<br></li><li>Illinois prohibits “ballot selfies,” so you can’t post a photo of a completed ballot on social media. But no one is stopping you from taking and posting a selfie with your “I Voted” sticker.</li></ul>

entries.title: Road rage blamed for Brighton Park shooting that left woman, 32, clinging to life, alder says
entries.summary: <p>Road rage apparently sparked a shooting attack that left a 32-year-old woman in critical condition Thursday morning in the Brighton Park neighborhood, Chicago police and an alderperson say.</p><p>The woman was a passenger in a vehicle in the 2400 block of West 47th Street about 9:30 a.m., when a gray car pulled up beside her and a someone inside opened fire, hitting her in the head, according to police. </p><p>The woman’s husband and two of their three children were also in the car, Ald. Raymond Lopez (15th) told the Sun-Times. Her husband is working with police to identify public and private surveillance cameras in the area, said Lopez, who added he believes road-rage sparked the shooting. </p><p>"As we get more information as to where this may have been originated. we’ll be asking for residents and businesses to check their cameras," Lopez said. </p><p>The woman was taken in critical condition to Mount Sinai Hospital and the shooter fled south on Western Avenue, police said.</p><p>In a Facebook post, Lopez said witnesses identified a gray four-door Toyota Scion with a rear bike rack as the shooter's vehicle. </p><p>No other injuries were reported and no arrests have been reported. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Shakespeare Theater chief Kimberly Motes to step down
entries.summary: <p>After three years as executive director at Chicago Shakespeare Theater, Kimberly Motes will step down in November. Motes will become President and CEO of Hennepin Arts in her hometown of Minneapolis, the company’s board announced this week.</p><p>In Motes' three years at Chicago Shakespeare Theater, she worked with Artistic Director Edward Hall to produce 35 plays and musicals, including 10 North American world premieres, and sending two productions to Broadway.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" entries.author: Mike Davis

entries.title: Bulls hoping that debut whooping in Toronto was rock bottom for rebuild
entries.summary: <p>Styles do indeed make the fight but the key ingredient in that statement having any truth is there has to be fight.</p><p>That’s maybe the most disappointing takeaway from the opener by the Bulls: No fight.</p><p>It was evident from the tip-off and felt through the entire building. A fight? These two opponents weren’t even in the same weight class.</p><p>Toronto was more physical, longer, more disruptive and carried out the butt-beating in methodical fashion. They were everything coach Tiago Splitter wants his Bulls team to be someday.</p><p>“The way we competed,” Splitter said of what disappointed him most in the 135-92 drubbing on Wednesday. “After a turnover, getting our heads down when running back, that’s something we cannot accept.”</p><p>The headliner in a list of things that cannot be accepted.</p><p>But before the white flags are prematurely hoisted on the 2026-27 campaign, some nuance in the first-round knockout delivered by the Raptors:</p><ul id="rte-6f4dafa0-ce4a-11f1-a435-b3d91a6419a0"><li> Toronto was possibly the worst matchup the Bulls could get in an opener just because of the length and physicality.</li></ul><ul id="rte-6f4dafa1-ce4a-11f1-a435-b3d91a6419a0"><li>Rookie Caleb Wilson wasn’t deterred by his slow start or his messy ball security game, competing until he was pulled from the game.</li></ul><ul id="rte-6f4dafa2-ce4a-11f1-a435-b3d91a6419a0"><li>Rebuilds hurt.</li></ul><p></p><p>Now comes an early-season test for this entire organization. First, how patient can Splitter be with a group that is yet to reflect his personality on the court?</p><p>As a player, Splitter grew up in the Spurs organization and with coach Gregg Popovich. It was a brand of basketball built on ball movement and unselfishness on the offensive end, and physicality and toughness on the defensive end.</p><p>Even in his one season as Portland’s interim coach last year, the Trail Blazers might not have had the skill as other teams on the offensive end, but they were a top defensive team that tried to make life difficult for the opponent on every possession.</p><p>This Bulls team is not that.</p><p>The hopeful return of Nic Claxton (hamstring) in a few weeks adds rim protection but does little in the physicality department. What Splitter has to lean on is using this team’s athleticism on the defensive side to cover up the lack of physicality.</p><p>Not an easy line to walk, especially against a team like the Raptors.</p><p>Secondly, how quickly can Game 1 be put in the rearview mirror with no lingering effects?<br>Besides Tre Jones and nine minutes of Zach Collins, no player on the roster should have come across the border on Thursday feeling like they played well.</p><p>Wilson had a nightmarish first half, Josh Giddey – who is now dealing with a minor left wrist issue – was far too passive in pushing the offense, and Matas Buzelis did get to the free throw line (13-of-16) but was 0-for-4 from three and let the Raptors frontcourt have their way.</p><p>Milwaukee isn’t Toronto. That’s the next opponent for the Bulls to erase what happened in the opener but also re-establish a baseline of how they want to play.</p><p>The Bucks lost their opener in Washington and are considered to be a basement dwelling team this year. If the Bulls can’t get a better sense of Splitter’s style of basketball in Milwaukee on Friday afternoon, then when?</p><p>The schedule is relentless for the next few weeks, facing Boston, New York and Philadelphia twice each, as well as defensive-minded teams like San Antonio, Atlanta and Cleveland.</p><p>Besides Milwaukee and the home opener against the Wizards on Saturday, it could be a very long three weeks if corrections aren’t made.</p><p>Was the opener against the Raptors simply rock bottom? Maybe, but either way Splitter’s patience will be tested with this group.</p>
