entries.title: Bears pay tribute to Mike Ditka on 'Thursday Night Football'
entries.summary: <p>Playing their first game since the man synonymous with their franchise died, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> paid tribute to Hall of Fame player and legendary coach Mike Ditka on Thursday night at Soldier Field.</p><p>The team stenciled a football with Ditka's No. 89 on it onto the northwest sideline. The team is wearing a matching patch over the hearts of their navy jerseys. </p><p>The Bears handed out fake mustaches to all fans and a headband in the style of Ditka's sweater vest to the first 10,000. They have scheduled a moment of silence before the national anthem. The Bears are playing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-inactives-vs-patriots-lb-t-j-edwards-out-with-hamstring-injury" target="_blank" >Patriots</a>, the same team Ditka beat in Super Bowl XX. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/wDOhJ7_sET4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Bears fans get Mike Ditka mustaches at Soldier Field"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Bears guard Jonah Jackson walked into the stadium wearing a long-sleeved No. 89 jersey. Ditka's number was the last one retired by the Bears.</p><p>Tom Borich and his 12-year-old grandson, Kieran Chucketts, both from Superior, Wisconsin, came to pay their respects.</p><p>"I've been a Bears fan since the 1960s, but I was always by myself in the land of Packers and Vikings fans. Until my son-in-law and grandson came into the picture. Now I've finally got some Bears fans to root with me. It's been a wonderful time," Borich said. "Ditka embodies the toughness of Chicago and the toughness of the Bears. We're excited to be here."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://x.com/jonahjackson73?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@jonahjackson73</a> reppin' Da Coach 🤝 <a href="https://t.co/7WjFZBbV1u">pic.twitter.com/7WjFZBbV1u</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2113379171120386551?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Pro Football Hall of Fame posted a Ditka display on a concourse at Soldier Field. Ditka, who had 4,503 receiving yards from 1961-66, was the first tight end ever inducted into the Hall.</p><p>Ditka died Oct. 9. No public memorial has been announced. Thursday night, then, stood as a fitting tribute.</p><p><i>Ashlee Rezin contributed.</i></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears should focus on modest upgrades with trade deadline fast approaching
entries.summary: <p>The Colts were 7-2 and in first place in the AFC South last November when they decided to go all-in.</p><p>In a trade that shocked the NFL world, the Colts traded two first-round picks and receiver Adonai Mitchell to the Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner, who had signed a four-year, $120.4 million extension just four months earlier.</p><p>The Colts won one more game the rest of the year, though, sunk by poor play, Gardner playing just four games due to injury and quarterback Daniel Jones tearing his Achilles tendon in early December. The Colts began this season 2-4. They lost the pitiful Titans on Sunday, and general manager Chris Ballard was fired shortly thereafter.</p><p>It’s easy to credit NFL teams that push their chips in to try for a playoff berth. The Colts are a reminder of what happens when it doesn’t work out.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> would be wise to keep them in mind as they search for reinforcements in the two-and-a-half weeks before the NFL’s Nov. 10 trade deadline. While the team doesn’t figure to package two first-round picks — they wouldn’t have done that even for the Raiders’ Maxx Crosby during the offseason — they’re likely to search for veteran help at a modest cost.</p><p>They should. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/21/patriots-qb-drake-maye-emerges-as-bears-qb-caleb-williams-main-rival-from-2024-nfl-draft-class" target="_blank" >Bears</a> only have quarterback Caleb Williams on his rookie deal for another year-and-a-half and an offense that seems built to win games long into the winter.</p><p>The defense, though, is another story, and where general manager Ryan Poles should keep his focus — so long as he doesn’t trade anything better than a fourth-round pick. He has to be more aggressive than he was last year, when his trade deadline addition was situational edge rusher Joe Tryon-Shoyinka.</p><p>The Colts and Bears aren’t completely analogous. Ballard was on thin ice once he drafted quarterback Anthony Richardson, a flop, fourth overall in 2023, while the Bears believe they’ve found their franchise quarterback.</p><p>Still, the Bears see in front of them exactly what the Colts did almost a year ago —room to climb the standings.</p><p>With the exception of the undefeated 49ers, no one in the NFC is particularly intimidating. That wasn’t the case even a month ago. The Rams, the preseason Super Bowl favorites, are 2-4 and in last place in the NFC West. The Eagles are 2-4, too, and were struggling— they’ve scored the fewest points in the NFC — even before quarterback Jalen Hurts was lost for the season with a scary blood clot issue.</p><p>The Cowboys, a popular preseason pick, have a losing record. The Super Bowl champion Seahawks are just 3-3. The NFC South leaders gave up 59 points to the Bears <br>in Week 1.</p><p>Then there’s the NFC North, where everyone is .500 or better but the division-leading Vikings are the most flawed team of the four. Their dominant defense has given up the fewest points in the NFC, but their offense has generated the fewest passing yards in the conference, too.</p><p>At 0-2 in NFC North play, the Bears have work to do to win the division again this year. The Bears won’t play another divisional game until Thanksgiving, though. Adding veteran help between now and then could make a difference.</p><p>Chargers defensive end Khalil Mack, who played for the Bears from 2018-21, is an obvious target. The team has shown interest in a reunion dating to March 2025, when the Bears’ social media team posted a defensive highlight reel days before free agency began that featured more clips of Mack than any other former player. The message to the video: “Leave Your Mark.”</p><p>Mack decided to stay with the Chargers, where he’s signed consecutive one-year free-agent deals. It’s only a matter of time before the winless Chargers decide to sell, though — having a bye this week figures to cement the direction they decide to take.</p><p>The Cardinals have been denying that they want to trade defensive end Josh Sweat since training camp. He has two sacks in the past three weeks but is signed through 2028.</p><p>The Bears could use help at cornerback, too, where Jaylon Johnson has been disappointing and Tyrique Stevenson has been a combination of injured and underwhelming. The Eagles’ Riq Woolen would make sense as a change-of-scenario player, as would a familiar face: Nahshon Wright. The NFL’s takeaways leader with the Bears last year signed a free-agent deal in March to join the Jets — and, despite being healthy, has yet to play a defensive snap for the Jets this year.</p><p>If the Colts decide to sell, and they should, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner — who, like Mack, is on an expiring, expensive contract — is worth a phone call.</p><p>Before the Colts fired Ballard, he bemoaned that he was “sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.” </p><p>The Colts showed what happened when going for it goes wrong. Playing for the Bears would be different — or at least Poles would have to hope so.</p>

entries.title: Bears’ inactives vs. Patriots: LB T.J. Edwards out with hamstring injury
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will be without mainstay linebacker T.J. Edwards on Thursday against the Patriots. It's Edwards' second consecutive game sidelined by a hamstring injury.</p><p>The Bears also will miss backup linebacker Jack Sanborn (concussion) and likely will start Devin Bush and D'Marco Jackson.</p><p>They won't have No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai for the third game in a row, leaving a share of the carries for Roschon Johnson. Monangai has been on the injury report with thumb and toe injuries, though coach Ben Johnson has said the thumb isn't a significant concern.</p><p>Those issues have kept him out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/04/bears-jets-qb-tyson-bagent-13-3-halftime-score-uneven-soldier-field-cairo-santos-case-keenum-nfl" >since rushing for 146 yards and two touchdowns on 30 carries</a> against the Jets on Oct. 4.</p><p>The good news for the Bears is that right guard Jonah Jackson will play through a hip injury that took him out of the Falcons game last week.</p><p>Here are the Bears' inactives:</p><p>QB Case Keenum*<br>RB Kyle Monangai (thumb, toe)<br>OL Jordan McFadden</p><p>DL Jayden Loving<br>LB T.J. Edwards (hamstring)<br>LB Jack Sanborn (concussion)<br>CB Nick McCloud</p><p>* - designated as emergency third quarterback</p>

entries.title: CPS board approves new lunchroom workers contract that raises wages
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education on Thursday approved a new contract with lunchroom staff after more than a year of negotiations, raising worker’s wage floors and warding off a strike.</p><p>Under the agreement lunchroom workers represented by Unite Here Local 1, including cooks and attendants, will receive raises to their current pay as well as increases based on their position and years of work. Wages were a key issue for the union as it has reported that many of the roughly lunchroom workers it represents had difficulties affording necessities under their last contract.</p><p>Unite Here Local 1 currently represents roughly 1,500 CPS lunchroom workers, according to the union.</p><p>All lunchroom staff will earn at least $21 an hour under the new agreement and associate managers can earn up to $27 an hour, according to Chicago Public Schools. Next summer, all employees will receive a 4% cost of living increase, followed by a 2.5% raise in 2028.</p><p>Previously, a vast majority of lunchroom workers were <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/27/cps-lunchroom-workers-wages-so-low-they-can-barely-feed-own-families-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>making $18.42 or less an hour,</u></a> according to the union. Average salaries ranged from about $23,400 to $37,400, according to CPS’ employee roster from earlier this year.</p><p>A survey the union <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/27/cps-lunchroom-workers-wages-so-low-they-can-barely-feed-own-families-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>conducted in 2025</u></a> found nearly half had trouble affording basic necessities, and 67% struggled to afford food at times. The survey also found that 22% of lunchroom workers received SNAP benefits and visited food banks.</p><p>An analysis<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/06/walmart-amazon-cps-top-employers-illinois-workers-still-need-snap-benefits-trump-work-requirements-lose-benefits" target="_blank" ><u> by the Chicago Sun-Times earlier this year</u></a> identified CPS among the top 10 employers statewide in terms of the number of their workers who receive SNAP food assistance.</p><p>Letia Downing-Lowe, a lunchroom attendant at Eli Whitney Elementary for 11 years, called the agreement a “breath of fresh air” and said lunchroom workers feel “more respected.”</p><p>“We’ve brought to the table so much more that we didn’t have,” said Downing-Lowe, who was also part of the union’s negotiating team.</p><p>Longtime workers like Downing-Lowe will see additional increases under the new contract. Those with 10 years of service will receive a $1 per hour raise and those with 20 years will see increases of $2 an hour, CPS said.</p><p>The deal also establishes a more “consistent” wage structure for lunchroom managers and cooks, according to the district. Their pay was previously based on the number of meals served at school.</p><p>The new agreement covers four years from July 2025 through June, 2029, and will cost the district nearly $65 million, CPS said. The district will have to make retroactive payments to honor the deal. The last contract expired in June 2025.</p><p>Wages and staffing levels were two of the biggest sticking points in negotiations, according to the union. CPS has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/15/cps-will-cut-teachers-and-five-student-non-attendance-days-as-district-looks-to-close-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>steadily decreased the number of lunchroom workers</u></a> as it deals with ongoing budget deficits.</p><p>Downing-Lowe hopes the new contract will lead to more applicants.</p><p>“Because the wages have gone up, hopefully we can hire new people and the staffing can get back to where it was,” Downing-Lowe said.</p><p>The union took escalating actions over the last few months as talks seemed to stall and it appeared a strike was on the horizon.</p><p>In April, union members <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/23/lunchroom-workers-plan-to-block-traffic-as-contract-talks-with-cps-stall" target="_blank" ><u>performed acts of civil disobedience</u></a> to “sound the alarm” on their need for a new contract. Several workers were detained by police after they sat in the street in front of CPS headquarters to call attention to their lack of a contract. Both sides had also agreed to call in a federal mediator who typically intervenes when talks have hit an impasse in order to prevent a strike.</p><p>And in July the union requested the start of a fact-finding process. That’s where a third party reviews arguments on both sides of a dispute and issues a report. Under state law school district workers aren’t allowed to strike until 30 days after the fact-finding report is released.</p><p>But the union and CPS reached a tentative agreement on Oct. 1 and it was ratified by the union on Oct. 11, according to the district.</p><p>At Thursday’s board meeting CPS Superintendent and CEO Macquiline King celebrated the deal.</p><p>“I thank our lunchroom employees for their dedication, I thank them for sticking it out with us and I'm glad an agreement has been reached that honors their commitment to our students and school communities,” King said.</p>

entries.title: ComEd's Lincoln Park substation shouldn't be built, judges say
entries.summary: <p>ComEd appears to have hit a setback with its proposal to build a substation in Lincoln Park — a plan that has drawn fierce pushback from neighborhood groups.</p><p>Administrative law judges for the Illinois Commerce Commission said in a filing last week that the utility giant didn't justify its need for the substation. The filing was a response to ComEd’s multiyear grid plan that includes building five substations. </p><p>ComEd has argued the new Lincoln Park substation is necessary to relieve capacity constraints and strengthen the grid. Its most recent forecasts show substations serving Lake View, North Center, Uptown and the northern part of Lincoln Park are projected to exceed 95% capacity by 2026, which the utility argues could result in brownouts, blackouts and less reliable service.</p><p>And ComEd wants to build <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/energy/2026/06/06/comed-plans-lincoln-park-substation-neighborhood-pushback" >a new substation</a> at 1111 W. Diversey Parkway, a former COVID-19 testing facility, to better serve those neighborhoods. </p><p>But the utility didn't convince judges at the ICC that a substation of its proposed size is needed. The three judges recommended the ICC consider a more “appropriately scaled project” in upcoming rate proceedings, if ComEd proposes one. </p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and the Citizens Utility Board also condemned the substation and its scale in their testimonies. </p><p>CUB argued a five-transformer substation would be overbuilding compared to power demand forecasts. It pointed to ComEd predicting a 3% load growth rate for the North Side in its proposed grid plan, compared to 6% growth between 2021 and 2025. That’s a “significant deceleration” that doesn’t justify three or more new transformers in Lincoln Park, CUB said.</p><p>ComEd said in a statement to the Sun-Times: "The [administrative law judges] did not reject the proposed location of the substation at 1111 W. Diversey. Rather, we understand them to be seeking greater clarification regarding the number of transformers needed to meet the needs of the community. Our grid plan indicates a need for three transformers. We are working to provide a more detailed look at the equipment within the substation needed to match the projected growth of the neighborhoods. Our goal remains to deliver that additional capacity reliably, cost-effectively and in a timely manner. We will continue to advocate for a Grid Plan that meets the evolving energy needs of the more than 400 communities we serve."</p><p>The judges’ recommendation is being heralded as a win by the Diversey Community Coalition, a neighborhood group formed earlier this year in response to ComEd’s substation proposal. The group mobilized more than 1,000 individuals to submit public comments to the ICC in opposition to the substation. It also held a September <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/24/lincoln-park-residents-rally-comed-substation" >rally</a> with lawmakers outside the proposed substation to draw more attention to the proposal.</p><p>“It is clearly time for ComEd to come to the table and work with the Coalition, our elected officials and the community on a different path forward that puts the community first,” the Diversey Community Coalition said in a statement.</p><p>Marie Poppy, one of the coalition's co-founders, said she isn’t surprised by the outpouring of public comments. </p><p>“We knew from talking with the community and the turnout at these community meetings” that people were passionate, Poppy said. “People are asking, ‘What can I do?’ These people felt really helpless.”</p><p>The coalition’s aim is to block the project so the land can instead be sold to a developer who would build housing.</p><p>The site is about 735 feet from the Diversey CTA station, making it an equitable transit-oriented development site. Streets within half a mile of a CTA or Metra train station or a quarter of a mile from a qualifying CTA bus line are eligible for a transit-oriented development designation, which opens up a developer's access to grants and<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/08/15/parking-requirements-cta-metra-transit-affordable-housing-crisis" target="_blank" ><u> reduces development costs</u></a>, according to the city.</p><p>Neighbors have been disappointed with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/energy/2026/06/23/north-side-neighbors-grill-comed-lincoln-park-substation-project" >ComEd’s response</a> to the coalition’s calls for a different location to be found.</p><p>The coalition, in partnership with local Ald. Timmy Knudsen (43rd) and consultants, found 14 alternative sites where a new substation could be built in the area. They included a Jewel-Osco parking lot on North Clybourn Avenue and a 1.2-acre lot on Diversey Parkway.</p><p>ComEd has rejected all of them.</p><p>Knudsen wrote a letter to ComEd in September asking it to answer 10 questions that would clarify how the utility evaluated the 14 sites. While ComEd responded to Knudsen, he said in a statement last week that “the reply falls short of delivering the robust, data-driven explanations requested, leaving several critical questions unaddressed.”</p><p>The deadline for the ICC to take action on ComEd's grid plan is Dec. 15 and would include the approval or rejection of the Lincoln Park substation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/22/data-centers-comed-3-billion-icc-consumer-groups-cub-illinois-households" >Data centers will cost ComEd $3 billion, but consumer groups worry Illinois households will be on the hook</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson announces plan to expand food access, create indoor public markets
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson wants to increase food access by creating a community-based “market city” framework, with priority attention given to the historically underserved South and West sides.</p><p>Johnson’s new plan, called the Market City Action Plan, was announced Thursday and would further his 2025 idea to establish a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/02/12/chicago-plan-open-city-grocery-store-changed-favor-public-farmers-markets" >public market</a>. It calls for creating administrative infrastructure to provide resources for food entrepreneurs, supporting existing farmers markets and building a network of year-round indoor public markets.</p><p>He also signed an executive order to establish a steering committee that would bring together city departments and community members to implement the plan. Johnson appointed Aaliayah Romer as manager of food equity to head the initiative.</p> <p>“Our Market City strategy is about building a food system that responds to what communities need while creating more opportunities for local entrepreneurs to grow and succeed," Johnson said in a news release. "This executive order moves that vision into action so we can deliver lasting solutions shaped by the needs of our neighborhoods.”</p><p>Johnson first floated the idea of expanding food access in 2023 when he proposed a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/2/23882682/mayor-brandon-johnson-city-owned-grocery-south-west-low-food-access-grocery-desert" >city-owned grocery store</a>. Following a feasibility study on the idea, he pivoted to opening public markets.</p><p>“After a very thoughtful and a more thorough engagement over the last several years, listening to people, we heard loud and clear that the entrepreneur spirit of Chicagoans wanted their efforts to be strengthened, and especially Chicago's existing food ecosystem. So it was important that we're building on the innovative work that's already happening in our neighborhoods,” Johnson told the Chicago Sun-Times Thursday.</p><p>Residents on the South and West sides statistically have much lower access to grocery stores than other neighborhoods. A report released this year by the Greater Chicago Food Depository found 51% of South Side homes, 45% of West Side homes and 41% of Southwest Side homes are food insecure and don’t have consistent access to enough food.</p><p>Johnson's announcement comes three months after the city-funded redevelopment deal with the operators of Save A Lot fell apart after the owner, Yellow Banana, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" >closed its seven stores</a> one year after opening.</p><p>Following the Save A Lot closures, the city announced in August that it would provide <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/08/31/chicago-neighborhood-market-10-000-grants-food-access-south-west-sides" >$450,000 in microgrants</a> through its Neighborhood Market Grant Program to help support existing grocers and markets.</p><p>Johnson's new plan was developed over the last year in collaboration with the Chicago Food Equity Council and the Greater Chicago Food Depository, as well as community stakeholders such as residents, entrepreneurs, farmers and market operators.</p><p>The mayor’s office said the next step will be to release a request for information to the public in the next month, with the goal of identifying potential sites and operators for a market.</p><p>Residents would likely see the first results of the plan through additional support to farmers markets during the 2027 season, said Ruby Ferguson, senior director of community engagement at the Greater Chicago Food Depository. The support could be financial or through marketing help.</p><p>Johnson said the city is still considering whether it will own or operate the public markets and that it may instead provide support.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/08/31/chicago-neighborhood-market-10-000-grants-food-access-south-west-sides" >Chicago offering $10,000 grants to help support food access on South and West sides</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" >Save A Lot stores set to close Saturday after years of turmoil, recent CEO death threatens city-funded deal</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks need to improve their breakouts, and thousand-gamer Ian Cole knows how they can
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> defenseman Ian Cole spent some of this week coordinating logistics with an entourage of family members coming to the United Center for his 1,000th career NHL game Friday.</p><p>The 37-year-old Michigan native has arguably <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/26/blackhawks-ian-cole-nhl-landon-slaggert-jeff-blashill" >improved</a> with age, and he's now set to reach one of hockey's most impressive milestones a month into his stint with his 10th different organization. It will be a special night for him.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill, who first met Cole when he was getting recruited to Notre Dame and later coached him with the Lightning, described Cole's weight-room workouts as a "great example" of the "day-to-day dedication that it takes to have longevity in this league."</p><p>But Cole spent an even larger portion of this week studying — along with the rest of the Hawks' defensemen — what's going wrong with their defensive-zone breakouts and how they can improve them.</p><p>Blashill took accountability Tuesday for not working on breakouts enough right away this season. Regardless, the Hawks' inability to consistently retrieve dump-ins and get the puck back out across the blue line (ideally with possession) has been backbreaking throughout their first nine games.</p><p>Three practices this week — as well as a number of "hard meetings" and video-review sessions — offered an opportunity to dig deep into the issue and get on the same page before hosting the Canadiens on Friday. </p><p>Considering the Hawks' next nine games will come rapid-fire in a 16-day span, they better be aligned now.</p><p>"It is objectively a tough job when somebody puts a bouncing puck into a corner and they're coming to hunt you," Cole said Thursday. "But that is our job, and we need to accomplish the job.</p><p>"We want to move [the puck] to our forwards as quickly as possible, with as much space as possible, with as much speed as possible. Then it becomes, 'If that's the end result we're looking for, how do we go about navigating the road to getting that?'"</p><p>It turns out the answer is extremely complicated. There aren't any foolproof strategies that will work every time, because every breakout presents a unique puzzle.</p><p>Cole did a remarkably good job explaining the science of breakouts in an easy-to-understand way.</p><p>"Guys have routes and they're coming back into certain spots, and the puck ends up in different spots. It's like this long equation that's constantly changing," he said.</p><p>"When you go get a puck, the variables may be different when you touch it than when you were skating to it. Maybe a guy peeled off and you'd be like, 'Now <i>this</i> is open.' These are things we need to train our brain to solve quickly."</p><p>Plus, the Hawks have to stay one step ahead of the opposition, who will watch for patterns and start anticipating and covering for anything the Hawks do more than once or twice.</p><p>"Sure, maybe a weak-side rim is the play, but it might not be the play every time," he added. "If their 'F3' goes and stands in front of our winger, we're going to rim it right to somebody. Maybe it's the strong side. Maybe it's a thing to the center. Maybe it's [time to] cut back and skate out of it. All these things are options. </p><p>"We need to do, as a team, a better job deciphering what those options are and when to use each option. That's what this week has been really good for. [We've been] going through those and saying, 'Here's a situation. What are your options? This guy is here instead of there. What are your options now?'"</p><p>If the Hawks' defensemen can nail this down, it should <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/16/blackhawks-forward-lineup-strategy-forechecking-puck-pressure" >sequentially lead</a> to more offense. </p><p>And that could help Cole finally earn his first point as a Hawk, even though production isn't what he's paid for. It would be fitting if it happened Friday.</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: The White Sox have openings in the outfield, and slugging prospect Caleb Bonemer is preparing to fill one
entries.summary: <p>There are some in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> player development who think 21-year-old prospect Caleb Bonemer looks like Mike Trout.</p><p>Not because he’s on a Hall of Fame trajectory, not yet. Not even after 39 home runs and counting this year through 143 games across the minors and the Arizona Fall League.</p><p>Rather, when he’s manning center field in Arizona despite a build more typical of a lead blocker for Bears running back D’Andre Swift, Bonemer <i>looks</i> like Trout, down to the Michigan native’s tree trunk of a neck and the deceptively suitable footspeed.</p><p>“The reads and the first step, and the lack of apprehension relative to some of the movements in the outfield were really encouraging,” White Sox farm director Paul Janish said of Bonemer’s transition to life on the grass.</p><p>Bonemer’s immolation of low minors pitching — he hit .251/.380/.550 across High-A and Double-A this year — earned him a midseason trip to the Futures Game in Philadelphia. As is often the case when seeing him for the first time, league scouts in attendance were troubled by the eerily still setup to his swing, where Bonemer’s only pre-pitch movement is a subtle load into his back hip. They quibbled about his actions on the infield, lining up with Bonemer’s admittedly shaky defensive performance that saw him commit 24 errors across shortstop and third base.</p><p>And scouts tended to note, as Bonemer posted plus run times from home to first, the power-hitting prospect is faster than he looks.</p><p>“Speed was always my game, and honestly this year with the added size, I kind of ticked that down a little bit,” Bonemer told the Sun-Times, noting the roughly 15 pounds he put on in added strength over the offseason. “Just playing in the outfield, I think it'll bring out some of that speed.”</p><p>They need starting pitching more, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/14/white-sox-will-pursue-starting-pitching-help-this-offseason-chris-getz-luis-castillo-davis-martin" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox general manager Chris Getz said he’ll seek outfield help this winter</u></a>. After leading MLB in slugging against left-handed pitching, Randal Grichuk will be a free agent this winter, as will Tommy Pham. The Sox hope to see Braden Montgomery mature into a franchise cornerstone in right field, but the rookie switch-hitter posted a .430 OPS against lefties last year, and both he and Sam Antonacci could use a right-handed complement.</p><p>Why not Bonemer? He’s not in Glendale on a fact-finding mission.</p><p>“From what I was told from Janish,” Bonemer said on Thursday. “Being able to play outfield, would only accelerate the process of hopefully playing in the big leagues.”</p><p>Few, if any, league evaluators expect Bonemer to stay in center, and the presence of Tristan Peters and Brenton Doyle on the Sox depth chart suggests the outfield corners are where he’ll find playing time on the 2027 team. But the added difficulty of center can only aid Bonemer’s development. It’s occasionally super-charged by the AFL experimenting with outfield positioning rules at Salt River Field in Scottsdale, forcing fielders to play shallower with corner outfielders hugging the lines.</p><p>“Pretty much every ball is pretty much over your head or in the gap,” said Bonemer, who as an infielder, is used to playing balls in front of him. “It’s a lot of running around.”</p><p>For that, Bonemer’s offseason regimen will contain more cardio training, since patrolling the outfield at the end of his first year of over 140 games played has been taxing. He wants to work on swing decisions, as his first half issues against breaking balls and a strikeout rate north of 26% can make him look like a little too natural of a fit with the boom-and-bust nature of the 2026 Sox offense.</p><p>Bonemer will be a rookie next year, not Mike Trout in waiting, so expectations should be kept in check. But if the Sox can find a way to wedge him into their defensive alignment, the ultimate appeal to his game is similar.</p><p>“A lot of homers, extra-base hits,” said Bonemer, summing up the strengths of his year. “Very pleased with that.”</p>
